name: Tara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a hoist operator at an underground nickel mine, which means I run the big winder at the top of the main shaft. The skips carry the ore up, and the cage carries the people down and back, about a kilometre each way. I'm the senior operator on day shift, so I sign off the shaft inspection, check the ropes and brakes with the electricians, and then I'm in the winder house most of the day watching the dials and the cameras. When the cage goes down with forty people in it, I'm the one holding them, and I don't forget that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the responsibility, and the quiet. The winder house is about the only quiet place on a mine. What wears me out is the sitting still, twelve hours of focus with your coffee going cold. My husband Mark is a fitter at the same mine, he fixes the pumps underground. I sing in the choir at St Peter's on Sundays, and on Saturdays I bake wedding cakes for people from church, a bit of extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most new things are like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, back to work. People get excited about new things and then they settle down. I'd probably say something like that after choir over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I use the AI on my phone sometimes, Mark's sister showed me, I asked it how to fix a sunken sponge once. It's useful, but I'd rather the winder stayed in human hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep putting money aside, we've got about four months of bills between us. Maybe take on a couple more wedding cakes in the summer, and start properly saving for a house with a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit relieved for Mark too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relieved for Mark. Why him especially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we're both at the same mine. If something goes wrong there, it goes wrong for both of us at once. Mum always said don't put all your eggs in one basket, and here we are, both eggs in the nickel basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the winder already automated in any way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ore skips mostly run themselves already, they've done for years. But when people are in the cage, the law says someone qualified is in the chair. That's me. I don't see that changing in a hurry.

S0.say: Well, that's that, back to work. People get excited about new things and then they settle down, and I'd say so after choir over tea.
S0.think: I'd be pleased, because the AI on my phone is useful but small. I'd rather the winder stayed in human hands.
S0.do: Carries on with the same shifts and keeps saving, at about four months of bills between her and Mark. Takes on a couple more wedding cakes in summer and starts saving for a house with a garden.
S0.feel: Calm, and relieved for her husband too.
S0.quote: Both eggs in the nickel basket.
S0.fieldNote: Tara carries a strong sense of duty for the people in the cage. Both she and her husband work at the same mine, which she knows is a shared risk. She uses AI only for small things at home, picked up from family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I can picture that. Slowly, like most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll adapt like our parents did, with hard work and looking after each other. I'd tell the younger ones to get their tickets and not wait. I wouldn't say much online, I keep that for church notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the winder will go remote, run from the control room in town, once the rules allow it. I'd probably keep a job, because they'll still want someone qualified. But Mark's job, fixing pumps, might change more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first remote hoist is running at another mine for a year, then ask for the training. I'd keep saving, and maybe push back the house until we know where we both stand. I'd make the cake business a bit more regular, maybe register it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just more careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to see it work with people in the cage, not just ore. I'm not going to be the first to trust it with forty lives. Once it's proven, I'll learn it, the same way I learned the new brakes three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ray, who trained me. He's sixty-one and he's been in that chair since before I was born. I'd want them to let him finish in the chair, not push him into a room full of screens at the end of his working life.

S1.say: We'll adapt like our parents did, with hard work and looking after each other. The younger ones should get their tickets and not wait.
S1.think: The winder will probably go remote once the rules allow it, and I'd likely keep a job because they'll still want someone qualified. Mark's pump work might change more than mine.
S1.do: Waits until a remote hoist has run for a year at another mine, then asks for the training. Keeps saving, may delay the house, and makes the cake business more regular, perhaps registering it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not scared but more careful.
S1.quote: I'm not going to be the first to trust it with forty lives.
S1.fieldNote: Tara will adopt remote hoisting once it's proven with people, not just ore. Her caution is rooted in her duty to the miners in the cage. She worries most about her older mentor and about her husband's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to pull together now, because the government won't be quick enough. I'd say we need to keep people working, even part-time, rather than just paying them to stay home. I'd say that at choir and at the school fete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Both of us at the same mine, both of us gone in the same year. Four months of bills is nothing when there's no next job to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Mark and I would stop the house savings and keep it all as an emergency fund. We'd cut the extras, the car upgrade, the trip to the coast. I'd bake as many cakes as people want, because weddings still happen, robots or not. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move in with them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when the cage stalls between levels and you wait for the radio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said weddings still happen. Do you think the cake business could carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not carry, no. It's about two hundred a month. But people want something made by hand for a wedding, and I think that lasts longer than most things. It's not a living, it's a lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Mark were thinking about children. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait, probably. I'd pray about it, honestly. My faith says God provides, but my head says don't bring a baby into no wages. I'd be torn, and I think we'd wait a year to see.

S2.say: Families and churches need to pull together now, because the government won't be quick enough. We should keep people working, even part-time, rather than paying them to stay home.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, with both of us at the same mine and both gone in the same year. Four months of bills is nothing when there's no next job to go to.
S2.do: Stops saving for the house and keeps it as an emergency fund, cutting the car upgrade and the coast trip. Bakes as many cakes as people order, considers moving in with her parents, and delays having children for about a year.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like waiting for the radio when the cage stalls between levels.
S2.quote: It's not a living, it's a lifeline.
S2.fieldNote: Tara's biggest fear is that two incomes from one mine vanish together. She turns to family, church and her cake business rather than government. Her faith and her practical sense pull in different directions over having children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it, though it's still not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given some warning, so let's use it well. Apprenticeships, training, and keeping towns together. I'd say that at the church meeting, and I'd want the council involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine for three years or so. The hoist goes remote, I learn it once it's proven, and I'm in town in an office. After that, I honestly don't know, and Mark's worse off than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep working and keep saving, aiming for eight months. I'd wait for the remote hoist to prove itself and then train on it. I'd push Mark to look at maintenance on the new robot gear, because someone has to fix them. And I'd register the cake business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning Mark. Would he agree with your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's stubborn, he'd want to stay with the pumps. But he listens in the end, usually after a long walk with the dog. I'd sit him down at the kitchen table with the numbers, the way my mum did with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be careful, which is how I like to be. With two years I'm rushing. With five, I can watch, then follow, then save. That's my pace.

S3.say: We've been given some warning, so let's use it well with apprenticeships, training and keeping towns together. I'd want the council involved.
S3.think: I'd be fine for three years or so, running the remote hoist from an office in town once it's proven. After that I honestly don't know, and Mark's worse off than me.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving towards eight months of bills, and trains on the remote hoist once it's proven. Pushes Mark to move into maintaining robot equipment and registers the cake business properly.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can carry.
S3.quote: With five, I can watch, then follow, then save. That's my pace.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches Tara's careful style of watching, following and saving. She takes charge of planning for both of them and expects to talk her husband round. She's clear she has no plan for after the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. We'd have kids by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it to plan properly, as families and as a town. Training, savings, apprenticeships, not panic. I'd say it to the young people at church especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel steadier with ten years. I'd probably have a long run in the chair or the remote room. The end point still worries me, but I'd have children and a home by then, and that changes what you're working for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, carry on, keep saving, and start trying for a baby like we planned. We'd buy a small house in two or three years. I'd do the remote hoist training when it's proven. And I'd keep the cakes going, because that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your children, if it happened when they were small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum used to hold forty people on a rope a kilometre long, and that mattered. And then I'd tell them God gives everyone a job to do, even if it's not a paid one. I'd want them to know their work is still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's mine, about the cakes. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine's not mine, the winder's not mine. The cakes are. If everything else goes to robots, I want something I make with my hands that people still ask for by name.

S4.say: Ten years is a blessing, and we should use it to plan properly as families and as a town. Training, savings and apprenticeships, not panic.
S4.think: I'd feel steadier with ten years and probably have a long run in the chair or the remote room. The end point still worries me, but children and a home change what you're working for.
S4.do: Carries on working and saving and starts trying for a baby in the first year. Plans to buy a small house in two or three years, trains on the remote hoist once proven, and keeps the cake business going.
S4.quote: I want something I make with my hands that people still ask for by name.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Tara goes ahead with children and a house and feels mostly at peace. Her faith frames work as worthwhile even if unpaid. The cake business matters to her as something she owns, not just extra money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Mark and I would both lose our work in the same year, with no time to be careful. What would help is keeping people in some kind of work, even part-time, and help through families and churches rather than just a payment from far away. And proper training for the remote jobs, paid by the company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples who work at the same place. It's common out here. If the mine goes, it's not one wage, it's both, and nobody plans for that.

headlineQuote: Mum used to hold forty people on a rope a kilometre long, and that mattered.
portrait: Tara Ziegler is 27 and the senior hoist operator on day shift at an underground nickel mine, responsible for the cage that carries miners a kilometre down. She's married to Mark, a fitter at the same mine, sings in her church choir and bakes wedding cakes on Saturdays for a little extra money. She uses AI now and then and adopts new tools once they're proven, especially when lives are involved. Through the scenarios her biggest fear is losing both incomes at once, and she turns to family, church and her cake business. With ten years she feels mostly at peace and goes ahead with children and a house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Mark would both lose their work in the same year with no time to be careful.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping people in some kind of work, even part-time, help through families and churches, and company-paid training for the remote jobs.
